title: RewardBench 2: Advancing Reward Model Evaluation
claim: A benchmark combines diverse unseen human-prompted domains with a multi-rejected scoring format that correlates with downstream use.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, domain icons then scoring flow then downstream outcomes
description: A three-panel horizontal figure. The left panel shows a 2x3 grid of rounded teal icon tiles labeled Math, Safety, Instruction Following, Focus, Ties and Factuality, captioned 'Unseen, human data across domains'. The middle panel is a flow. A white Prompt card (write a poem where every sentence starts with A) points with arrows to a green Chosen card and a stack of orange/red Rejected cards, noting multiple incorrect answers per prompt. Both feed a pink Reward model box. To its right, the chosen score 0.5 appears with rejected scores 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, plus the rule 'RM is correct if chosen > all rejected'. The caption reads 'Score reward models with best-of-4 accuracy'. The right panel is a lavender box labeled Downstream RM Use, showing Best-of-N and PPO mini diagrams. Arrows lead from high and low scoring RMs to smiley and frowny faces, captioned 'Correlated with downstream use'.
caption: \evalname is composed of high-quality, unseen human prompts designed for a best-of-4 reward model evaluation format with completions generated from a variety of leading AI models. We extend RM evaluation of pairwise "chosen" and "rejected" completions to include additional rejected samples as distractions. \evalname has 6 domains which expand upon challenging domains in existing RM evaluations and adds a new domain, Ties, to test how RMs handle questions with multiple correct answers. The new data and setup enables more accurate correlation of benchmark scores with downstream performance via RL finetuning or best-of-N sampling.
abstract: Reward models are used throughout the post-training of language models to capture nuanced signals from preference data and provide a training target for optimization across instruction following, reasoning, safety, and more domains. The community has begun establishing best practices for evaluating reward models, from the development of benchmarks that test capabilities in specific skill areas to others that test agreement with human preferences. At the same time, progress in evaluation has not been mirrored by the effectiveness of reward models in downstream tasks -- simpler direct alignment algorithms are reported to work better in many cases. This paper introduces RewardBench 2, a new multi-skill reward modeling benchmark designed to bring new, challenging data for accuracy-based reward model evaluation -- models score about 20 points on average lower on RewardBench 2 compared to the first RewardBench -- while being highly correlated with downstream performance. Compared to most other benchmarks, RewardBench 2 sources new human prompts instead of existing prompts from downstream evaluations, facilitating more rigorous evaluation practices. In this paper, we describe our benchmark construction process and report how existing models perform on it, while quantifying how performance on the benchmark correlates with downstream use of the models in both inference-time scaling algorithms, like best-of-N sampling, and RLHF training algorithms like proximal policy optimization.
